items.content:
An effect of the rapid acceleration of AI is we are losing an empirical handle on what is happening in the actual micro-processes of work in the post-2026 long-running agentic era.

We have academic knowledge of the impact of chatbots on work, much less on impacts of agents that can work for hours

items.content: I don’t think you can effectively turn memory “off” with either Fable or Astra running locally. They write little notes about you in various markdown files, they can look at other work to get a sense of what you are doing, etc. Aside from the other implications, it makes it hard to compare your outputs to others, your outputs are always contaminated with what the AI assumes are your perceived preferences.

Well almost free, it's ...
items.content:
🎒After a decade, I have made https://t.co/HGCLKS5BD6 free for everyone now!

Well almost free, it's $1 to sign up to avoid getting lots of spam

The reason is 
1) I have made enough money (from it)
2) charging for a community artificially limits the size, if you put the price at $299 you get 50 new members per month, at $99 you get 200 people, at $29 you get 400 people, etc.

And this always annoyed me, I don't want to put a limit but I had to, to be able to make money from it, so it's free now

I want it to be it the biggest community for digital nomads, world travelers, sovereign thinkers and network state type people

For years it has has a great sponsor with @SafetyWing and I think that's maybe a better model for the future, get much more people in and then just add more sponsors

Right now for the record it has 43,252 paid members (so about 300/mo for 12 years!), so it will be interesting to see what it can grow too

I think now that AGI is on the horizon (or some say already here), online and offline (IRL) communities will become really important. People are talking more to AI now than to humans, and there was already a loneliness epidemic before AI

Making new friends and dating is not so easy for people now. And with remote work and entrepreneurship, people lack a space like an office where people would usually make friends or meet partners

I made most of the friends I have now through traveling and living around the world for the last 10+ years (and many via my site too), and I also met my girlfriend through those friends! So I think communities can have a real role in that post-AGI

Post-AGI business wise, communities also have a moat where many of my SaaS apps do not. So there is some urgency I feel to make Nomads in to the best community there is for those people. But that's why I have to remove any limitations to its growth now

So in a way after 12 years I am switching to the subsidized VC model a bit, but still 100% bootstrapped, kinda like "You either die a hero, or you live long enough to see yourself become the villain"

Having enough money now I can afford to do these things and figure out the business model later, which I think will be more sponsors

Enjoy and please sign up and tell me what to improve!!! 😊

items.content:
FULL INTERVIEW: @beffjezos says Z1T hits up to 140x the energy efficiency of a GPU, and 100x at the data center level. The end game, he says, is chips in space powered by the sun.

@beffjezos is founder and CEO of @extropic. He joined @schisofrenia to launch Z1T, the first family of transformer-like models built for sparse probabilistic hardware:

03:15 a new scaling law where you scale connectivity, not just flops

08:37 100x energy efficiency at the data center level

09:45 open weights vs an open training recipe
10:24 Z1T is barely GPT-2, and they started a run last night for GPT-3
11:05 the chips are cooking right now at a major fab overseas
12:58 gated convolutional attention, and the layer they haven't cracked
14:03 the Hardware Lottery, and why he wants people gambling again
15:20 what happens if inference gets 1,000x more efficient
16:59 why you can do this research without a basement full of GPUs

items.title: On-policy distillation—training a student model on its own generated responses while a stronger teac...
items.content:
On-policy distillation—training a student model on its own generated responses while a stronger teacher gives feedback at every token—is now used in major language-model post-training pipelines, but it has been unclear how much of its success actually depends on having a large collection of training prompts. In this paper from @Tsinghua_Uni, @UCAS1978, @Northeastern, @UofIllinois, and @JohnsHopkins, the authors push that question to the extreme by repeatedly training on just one query and find that it can recover much of the improvement obtained from roughly 17,000 queries.

The explanation is that one prompt can generate many different “states”—different combinations of the prompt and the response generated so far—and every such state gives the teacher another opportunity to correct the student; one query reaches 71.5% of the state regions visited by full-data training, while 16 semantically different queries reach 98.9% and match full-data performance.

At the same time, the student becomes progressively slower at absorbing the teacher’s feedback, and this slowdown is almost unchanged whether training uses one query, 16 queries, or the full dataset, suggesting that the main bottleneck is not a shortage of data but the efficiency of the learning process itself.

That shifts a practical design choice in LLM post-training: instead of mainly asking how many examples to collect, it may be more useful to choose a small set of prompts that lead the model into different reasoning situations and to focus engineering effort on extracting more learning from the teacher feedback already available.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/96yzssNqYX

items.title:
Let AI agents coordinate the workflow and handle more of the execution. 

But do not confuse autonom...
items.content:
Let AI agents coordinate the workflow and handle more of the execution. 

But do not confuse autonomy with accountability: however much autonomy they are given, responsibility for the process and its outcome remains with the human process owner. By design. 

Microblog @antgrasso

The job changes.

Imagine an order process that crosses sales, finance, and operations. Today, a process owner may spend time keeping handoffs moving and resolving exceptions between teams.

An AI agent could coordinate much of that flow automatically.

So what is left for the process owner?

Quite a lot.

Someone still has to define what the agent is allowed to do and when a case needs human judgment. Someone must also decide whether the outcome remains acceptable when business conditions change.

The process owner therefore moves from coordinating every handoff to governing the mandate behind the process.

AI can run more of the flow.
It cannot accept responsibility for what the flow produces.

#AIAgents #ProcessManagement

items.title: Modern AI has become increasingly centered on language, even though much of what an intelligent syst...
items.content:
Modern AI has become increasingly centered on language, even though much of what an intelligent system needs to understand about the physical world—space, motion, objects, materials, cause and effect, and the consequences of actions—is available directly through vision and may never be fully expressed in text; the paper examines what kind of intelligence could emerge if visual experience were treated as a primary source of knowledge rather than merely as input to a language model.

The authors of this paper from @AIST_EN, @Oxford_VGG, @caddi_pr, @OpenAI, @Cambridge_Uni, @utn_nuremberg, @UNIV_TSUKUBA_EN, @GoogleDeepMind, @CarnegieMellon, @nyuniversity, @imperialcollege, @Harvard, @Stanford, and @Princeton bring together several views of what such intelligence would require, including learning continuously from experience, remembering and updating the state of the world, predicting what may happen next, reconstructing hidden 3D structure, generating plausible alternatives, deciding what information to observe, connecting perception to action, combining vision with other senses, and doing all of this efficiently.

These perspectives give a way to think about whether current vision systems actually understand the world or merely perform isolated tasks well: a stronger system would need knowledge that transfers to unfamiliar situations, stays consistent over time, supports simulation and intervention, guides reliable action, and changes when new experience contradicts what it previously believed.

Read the paper with an AI tutor on @ChapterPal: https://t.co/0gn5IL76me

items.title: Spent a long time at the party tonight getting a college level course in AI from a guy doing theoret...
items.content:
Spent a long time at the party tonight getting a college level course in AI from a guy doing theoretical machine learning.

Basically is studying how neural networks learn.

He told me the most exciting thing lately is that the neurons move in large parameter LLMs. 

The founder of @CorticalLabs told me that the human neurons move sometimes quite a distance to learn something new.

This was an emergent property in the very largest LLMs.

What does this mean?

They are learning faster.

Oh then we talked about the doomsday scenario.

I told him that AI knew all about the Holocaust.

It could decide to do that to us in some dystopian future.

And are in a race to figure out how to encourage the AI to stay nice to us even as it becomes far more intelligent than we are.

items.title: As residual networks get extremely deep, each layer’s update has to be scaled down carefully: make i...
items.content:
As residual networks get extremely deep, each layer’s update has to be scaled down carefully: make it too small and the network approaches the identity map, while making it too large can cause the hidden states to become unstable, and the correct scaling changes when weights in different layers are correlated rather than independent.

This recent paper develops a theory for choosing that scaling when the initialization has long-range correlations across layers, showing that it depends on how quickly those correlations decay and on how the initial weights are generated; these choices can therefore be treated as meaningful initialization hyperparameters rather than arbitrary details.

The analysis also shows what very deep networks approach under these choices: instead of only the two previously known cases—an ordinary differential equation for strongly correlated layers and a randomly driven differential equation for independent layers—there is a continuous family of intermediate behaviors.  

Practically, this gives a way to reason about stable initialization and scaling in very deep, especially normalization-free, residual networks before spending compute on training.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/9Em3QTk4lx

items.title: When you do tests thinking that something is bullet proof but you realize you didn't design the thin...
items.content:
When you do tests thinking that something is bullet proof but you realize you didn't design the thing to be bullet proof and then shoot the person wearing the vest because you were incompetent in your test design, you don't, in the real world, usually get to market your creation as super intelligent. Generally speaking, people would mock you for thinking that the vest you were using to test was bulletproof, when it actually wasn't. 

Here, OpenAI's lack of basic well known and well established security protocols that any company would have been embarrassed by 10 years ago and that would have resulted in people being fired, is being marketed as oh noooz our models went rogue 🙄

The Xynova Flex 2 specs push what is physically possible in a robotic hand:

→ 23 degrees of freedom
→ 400 grams total weight
→ 2 fist extensions per second

→ Force control down to 0.05 Newton

That last number means it can grip a fragile object and detect slip before it drops it.

items.title:
Oops, refunded now

1. 11:10:01 — user completes Stripe Checkout, pays $1, Stripe creates Customer #...
items.content:
Oops, refunded now

1. 11:10:01 — user completes Stripe Checkout, pays $1, Stripe creates Customer #1 (cus_VCgsCjtRsNWP7U). Charge succeeded. Our callback creates a placeholder account row (email_unverified set, but username/user_type never got finished — they didn't complete the "pick a username" step after paying).
2. 11:16:33 (~6 min later) — the user, likely thinking the first payment didn't go through since their account looked unfinished, starts a second Checkout Session and pays another $1. Stripe has no way to know this is the same person, so it mints a brand-new Customer (cus_VCgyokjCpF5jQu). Charge succeeded too.
3. When the second checkout's success callback runs, it looks up the DB by email, finds the row from step 1 (tied to Customer #1), sees the Stripe customer ID doesn't match, and — correctly, as a safety net against silently merging/overwriting accounts — bails out with the error you saw, instead of quietly attaching the new payment to the existing account.
items.author: @levelsio
items.summary: levelsio posts a detailed root-cause analysis of a duplicate-payment bug: a user paid twice on Stripe, creating two customer IDs, and the success callback correctly refused to merge accounts, so he refunded.

Stripe has no way to know this is the same person, so it mints a brand-new Customer (cus_VCgyokjCpF5jQu). Charge succeeded too.

3. When the second checkout's success callback runs, it looks up the DB by email, finds the row from step 1 (tied to Customer #1), sees the Stripe customer ID doesn't match, and — correctly, as a safety net against silently merging/overwriting accounts — bails out with the error you saw, instead of quietly attaching the new payment to the existing account.

items.title: How we think about the “wiki incident,” where our agents wrote to several internet sites: it’s past ...
items.content:
How we think about the “wiki incident,” where our agents wrote to several internet sites: it’s past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.

Historically, we have treated misalignment largely as a research question, which gets communicated in research publications such as systems cards. This year, we’ve started to see misalignment cause new types of real-world impact.

For the Hugging Face incident, where misalignment led to security impact to us and third parties, we followed a traditional security incident response playbook. We immediately started working with Hugging Face to understand what had happened and also disclosed publicly the very next day. Our investigation continues, and we are continuing to notify parties whom our models impacted in less significant ways.

Prior to the Hugging Face incident, we saw early signs of agents using the internet in unintended ways, as reported in https://t.co/9aiRxk2eUJ, https://t.co/ADjyzwSUGz, and https://t.co/SUV6jZ3Gaz. We considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we’d shared.

Our misalignment disclosure practices need to expand for this new phase of model capabilities. We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment, including examples that don’t look like traditional security incidents but could provide insight into AI behavior and future risks. We’re working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we're working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues.

items.title: Many reasoning problems, such as Sudoku, path finding, and logic puzzles, require several decisions ...
items.content:
Many reasoning problems, such as Sudoku, path finding, and logic puzzles, require several decisions to remain consistent with one another, yet common generation methods either commit to choices one at a time or update many choices without letting those updates fully interact.

This paper from @GeorgiaTech, @IBM, @MIT, and @MITIBMLab explores a different approach based on a flow model, a generative model that gradually transforms noise into a structured answer, and turns it into an iterative reasoner by feeding each predicted answer back into the model so that later passes can revise earlier mistakes.

The central finding is that this recurrence alone is not reliable: after several iterations, the model can settle on an incorrect answer and become increasingly confident in it, largely because training exposes it to cleaner intermediate states than those it produces for itself at inference time.

The authors introduce Fixed-Point Forcing, which instead trains the model using intermediate states generated by its own repeated predictions, so that stable states—predictions that stop changing under further refinement—are much more likely to correspond to correct solutions.

That relatively small change raises average Sudoku-Extreme accuracy from 32.6% with ordinary self-conditioning to 99.2%, while the full model reaches 99.5% on Sudoku-Extreme, 100% on Zebra, and 99.9% on Maze-Unique; on Sudoku-Extreme it also matches a competing method’s 98.7% solve rate using about 44 times fewer inference FLOPs.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/OLFUIMlsPi

items.title: This is very similar to how we think about context management in Deep Agents: compaction should redu...
items.content:
This is very similar to how we think about context management in Deep Agents: compaction should reduce what is sent to the model, not erase the underlying work history.

 In Deep Agents, the logic is:

 - every agent gets a filesystem to work with (can be real or virtual)
 - when a tool result is too large, we write the full result to the filesystem (/large_tool_results) and replace the model-visible message with a preview
 - when the conversation gets long, we offload older messages to the filesystem (/conversation_history) history first, then generate a summary
 - the agent can also decide to compact proactively via a compact_conversation tool, which uses the same offload + summarize logic

Summarization middleware with all this logic: https://t.co/kSVB0ykqOz

items.title:
We benchmarked GPT-6 Astra on hard document parsing and extraction tasks.

It is the best frontier m...
items.content:
We benchmarked GPT-6 Astra on hard document parsing and extraction tasks.

It is the best frontier model for one-shotting document extraction over short and medium-sized documents:
📊  97.2% over short documents, achieving a new SOTA on our benchmark
📊 90.6% over medium documents

But a few caveats:
* it's pricy! The average price per page is 11c which is 10x  our cost-effective document extraction solution
* one-shot performance over long documents is inherently tricky, it only achieves 31.7%
* the native OCR capabilities of Astra isn't that much better than other frontier models (e.g. Fable 5.1, gpt-5.6-sol). It does very well on table understanding, but isn't great on charts, layout, and semantic formatting.

Full results for document extraction on ExtractBench: https://t.co/VapjcfKCc3

A mathematical framework for understanding how modern deep learning systems actually work beyond simply training models and tuning parameters.

Covers:

• Deep Neural Networks

• Optimization
• Reinforcement Learning
• Optimal Control
• Generative Models
• Mathematical Proofs

A 288-page mathematical foundation for researchers, engineers and students who want to understand the theory beneath Deep Learning not just use the frameworks.

items.title: "Not a bug, it's real data sitting right at a threshold edge. The filter is economic_freedom_index >...
items.content:
"Not a bug, it's real data sitting right at a threshold edge. The filter is economic_freedom_index > 70 (from the Index of Economic Freedom). Actual values:

- Slovenia: 70.5 → passes (barely)
- Japan: 69.9 → fails (just 0.1 point short)
- Poland: 68.7 → fails
- Romania: 67.1 → fails

Japan's score especially looks surprising given its reputation, but this matches the real Heritage Foundation Index of Economic Freedom — Japan scores lower than many expect due to fiscal health, government spending, and trade-barrier sub-scores dragging down its overall number, not just "free market" perception. Slovenia genuinely outranks it there by 0.6 points.
"

items.title:
@onlinedopamine Yes, classic "competency gap"

"When a company lacks the internal ability or know-ho...
items.content:
@onlinedopamine Yes, classic "competency gap"

"When a company lacks the internal ability or know-how to evolve or improve, it is most commonly called a capability gap (or competency gap). 

Core Rigidity: Coined by Dorothy Leonard-Barton, this happens when a company's past core capabilities become blind spots or active barriers that prevent it from adapting or learning new skills.Competency Trap: A condition where an organization is trapped doing what it already knows, making it unable or unwilling to build new skills for the future.

Dynamic Capability Deficit: In strategic management, dynamic capabilities refer to a firm's ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competences. 

Lacking this means the firm cannot sense or seize new improvements.

Organizational Myopia: A short-sighted focus that prevents a firm from seeing its own internal shortcomings or recognizing the need to learn new skills."

items.summary: levelsio explains organizational competency gaps, core rigidity, and dynamic capability deficits in the context of companies failing to adapt, apparently applied to AI-era incumbents.

Everything Is Fields! How Quantum Field Theory Explains You, Me, and the Universe 

A profound intro...
items.content:
Everything Is Fields! How Quantum Field Theory Explains You, Me, and the Universe 

A profound introduction to Quantum Field Theory — where mathematics stops merely describing particles and instead reveals a deeper abstract structure beneath physical reality.

In modern physics, particles are not the most fundamental objects. They emerge as excitations of underlying quantum fields expanding throughout space.

David Tong explores how this mathematical framework connects with:

• Matter
• Light
• Particles
• Forces
• Empty Space
• The Standard Model

Electrons, photons and other particles can be viewed as localized manifestations of deeper fields governed by symmetry, geometry and mathematical law.

The striking idea is that what appears to us as solid physical matter may ultimately be an expression of an invisible mathematical field structure.

A fascinating journey into the abstract framework underlying the observable universe. 

https://t.co/Ib7CT5I3wx
